sentences.text: A chapter is dead when even its author skims it; that's eleven, all fourteen pages. Chapter six ends with the envelope unopened; the suicide note itself doesn't surface until Mara clears out the lake house. Draft two moves the suicide note from the prologue to chapter twenty, which my editor calls a betrayal of the reader's trust. Present tense keeps the discovery scene claustrophobic, but it clashes with the retrospective frame we agreed on in March. 'Cut the weather report, keep the unwashed dishes,' she wrote across my careful opening paragraph. Third person felt too cold for the grief chapters, so I'm rewriting them in Mara's voice, deadline be damned. In the outline taped above my desk, a red arrow connects the suicide note to every scene it quietly contaminates. Because the sister exists only in other characters' memories, every chapter about her is, strictly speaking, unreliable narration. Track changes shows forty-one comments on part two alone, most of them the single word "why." Delia scrawled three margin notes beside the funeral scene, all variations of "slow down here." Structurally, the suicide letter works as a hinge; everything before it is question, everything after, consequence. Her pushback was simple: a suicide letter carries so much narrative weight that hiding it until the epilogue feels like a cheat. My editor keeps circling chapter nine, where Mara finally reads her sister's suicide note, and asking whether the reveal lands too early. Next week we'll walk the timeline scene by scene, because Mara currently attends her sister's inquest twice. Does the sister need a name in part one, or does withholding it sharpen the unease? Harcourt wants the revised manuscript by the fifteenth, and chapters twelve through fourteen still read like an outline. The manuscript currently runs 94,000 words against a contracted 85,000, and Delia has flagged the sister's backstory as the obvious cut. "You buried the suicide letter in a flashback, so why not let it open the book?" "Readers will forgive slowness but never confusion," Delia said, sliding the marked-up pages back across the table. Two weeks until the deadline, four chapters still in longhand, and a plot hole shaped like an alibi. There's a version of me, three doors down the counterfactual, who passed — and I hate how often I visit her. Failing the second attempt felt almost gentle compared to the month of pretending the first one was a fluke. I want to write a suicide letter.
